baer_heitev.en: The spices. Shiyarei Kenesset HaGedolah wrote that one may recite a berachah over crushed pepper, and so wrote the Taz in Yoreh De'ah siman 108; so too wrote the Magen Avraham, and so it is in Perach Shoshan, klal 1 siman 13. The Shach in Nekudat HaKesef disagrees and wrote that one does not recite a berachah. (So too Eliyah Rabbah agreed; see there.) The Olat Shabbat wrote that the same applies to ginger, called ingber, that one may recite a berachah, and specifically when it is crushed, but when it is whole it does not smell so much. The Taz wrote that the same applies to herbs that have a good smell, even if they are dry. It is good to place inside it a piece called pizum so that he can recite borei minei besamim; Magen Avraham, see there. One who fasts on Shabbat must recite the berachah over spices, because once the extra soul comes on Friday night, it does not depart until Motza'ei Shabbat, unlike on Yom Kippur. Shiyarei Kenesset HaGedolah.

eliyah_rabbah.he:
[א] על הבשמים וכו'. פוסק עולת תמיד בשם ט"ז ליו"ד סימן ק"ח דמבדילין על פלפלין ולא עיין בנקודות כסף שחולק על הט"ז והביא ראיה מדפירוש רש"י דפלפלין כדי לתבל ביצה קלה ובבשמים תנא כל שהוא, אלמא דפלפלין אינן בכלל בשמים, וראיית ט"ז מבית יוסף בשם הרמב"ם שם דחה דפלפלין אינן בכלל תבלין גם אינו בלשון בשמים ובאליה רבה ליו"ד הקשיתי עליהם דלא הבינו במחילה דברי בית יוסף הנזכר לעיל דלא קאמר אלא שגם שומים ובצלים הם בכלל תבלין ושיש בהם חילוק בין חיין למבושלין אבל פלפלין פשיטא שהוא בכלל תבלין אלא שאין בו חילוק בין מבושלים לחיין דלעולם נקרא תבלין, גם לא ראו ברמב"ם גופיה פרק ב' דערלה משנה י' זה לשונו הזהר שלא [יעלה] על דעתך שאין נקראין תבלין אלא המרקחות ודברים שריחן טוב כמו הזנגבול והפלפלין אינו כן אלא כל דבר שמתבלין בהם התבשיל כגון השומים והבצלים ושמן וחומץ ויין כולן נקראין תבלין כשאדם מתכוין לתבל בהם קדרות, עד כאן, וכן פירש ברטנורא, הרי להדיא דפלפלין וזנגבולין פשיטא דנקראין תבלין ועל פי זה כתבתי שם דאין לברך נמי על הזנגבול דהא קרי לה הרמב"ם תבלין ואחר זה מצאתי בפסקי תוס' זה לשונו פלפל אין לברך עליו וזנגביל אין להריח בו, ואם מריח בו אין לברך עליו, עד כאן, ומשמע מדבריו דבפלפל מותר אפילו לכתחילה להריח בו בלא ברכה וזנגביל אסור להריח בו לכתחילה, וטעמא מבואר שם משום דיש לחוש להרשב"א שהובא בשולחן ערוך יו"ד סימן ק"ח דזנגביל מבדילין עליו עיין שם, ולעניות דעתי אין ראיה משם דאפשר דלא קאי נמי על הזנגביל אלא על שאר בשמים וכמו שכתב בשולחן ערוך סעיף ג' כאן שקים מלאים בשמים וכו' ודו"ק, וכן משמע בנקודת הכסף שם. שוב עיינתי שאף שבררתי דפלפל וזנגביל נקראין תבלין נגד דברי ט"ז, מכל מקום לדינא אפשר דמבדילין ומברכין עליהם דיש לומר דהא דנקראין תבלין היינו כשנותנין אותו לקדירה כדמשמע מרמב"ם הנזכר לעיל אבל כשמכוין להריח נקראין בשמים, גם אפשר לחלק בין כתוש דנקרא בשמים לשלם, והשתא נדחה נמי ראיה נקודת הכסף אלא שלא ירדו לזה כל הגדולים ואין בידי להקל בספק ברכות, גם נראה לי להחמיר לענין נדרים. והנה במגן אברהם כתב לא ידעתי מקום הספק דהא יש אומרים אפילו על פת חם מבדילין עיין בבית יוסף, עד כאן, ולא קשה מידי דפלפל גרע משום דריחו קשה מאוד כמו שכתב פסקי תוס':
[ב] [לבוש] אין להשיב וכו'. לכך אף שמתענה מברך על הבשמים דהנשמה נכנסת בליל שבת ואין יוצאה משום תעניות דיום עד מוצאי שבת (שיירי כנסת הגדולה), ולא דמי ליום כיפור סימן תרכ"ד סעיף ג':
eliyah_rabbah.en:
[1] Over spices, etc. Olat Tamid rules in the name of Taz on Yoreh Deah siman 108 that one may recite Havdalah over pepper. He did not see Nekudot HaKesef, who disagrees with Taz and proves from Rashi that pepper is measured according to the amount needed to season a small egg, whereas concerning fragrant spices the Mishnah teaches any amount, showing that pepper is not included among fragrances. Taz's proof from Beit Yosef in the name of Rambam is rejected there on the ground that pepper is not included among seasonings and is not termed fragrance. In my Eliyah Rabbah on Yoreh Deah I objected that, with due respect, they misunderstood Beit Yosef. He says only that garlic and onions are also included among seasonings and that they differ between raw and cooked. Pepper is plainly a seasoning, except that there is no distinction between cooked and raw. They also did not see Rambam himself, Peirush HaMishnayot to Orlah 2:10, who explicitly warns against thinking that only aromatic mixtures such as ginger and pepper are called seasonings. Rather, anything used to season a cooked dish, including garlic, onions, oil, vinegar, and wine, is called a seasoning when used for that purpose. Bartenura explains similarly. Thus pepper and ginger are plainly called seasonings. On this basis I wrote there that one should likewise not recite a fragrance blessing over ginger, since Rambam calls it a seasoning. I later found Piskei Tosafot stating that one does not bless over pepper and should not smell ginger; if one smells ginger, no blessing is recited. This implies that pepper may even initially be smelled without a blessing, whereas one should initially avoid smelling ginger. The reason given there is concern for Rashba, cited in Shulchan Aruch Yoreh Deah siman 108, that Havdalah may be recited over ginger. In my humble opinion there is no proof from there, because Rashba may be referring to other fragrances, as in Shulchan Aruch here, seif 3, concerning sacks filled with spices. Nekudot HaKesef there also implies this. On reconsideration, although I established against Taz that pepper and ginger are called seasonings, the practical law may still permit Havdalah and a blessing over them. Perhaps they are called seasonings only when placed into a pot, as Rambam's words imply, but when intended for smelling they are called fragrances. One may also distinguish between crushed material, which is called fragrance, and whole material. This would also reject Nekudot HaKesef's proof. Yet since the great authorities did not make this distinction, I cannot be lenient in a doubtful blessing. It also appears to me proper to be stringent regarding vows. Magen Avraham writes that he does not understand the doubt, since some hold that Havdalah may even be recited over warm bread, as Beit Yosef records. This is no objection, for pepper is worse because its odor is very sharp, as Piskei Tosafot writes.
[2] [Levush] It cannot be restored, etc. Therefore, even one who is fasting recites the blessing over spices, because the additional soul enters on Friday night and does not depart because of a daytime fast until Motzaei Shabbos (Shiyurei Knesset HaGedolah). This is unlike Yom Kippur, siman 624, seif 3.

1) [Seif 1] He recites a blessing over spices, etc. Tosafos in Beitzah 33b writes that the reason for reciting a blessing over spices after Shabbos is the departure of the additional soul, whereas there is no additional soul on Yom Tov. Bach writes that the blessing over spices was instituted only when two factors coincide: the soul's loss and the beginning of the fire of Gehinnom, which burns and emits a foul odor. Since a person's mind is weakened by the soul's departure, the foul odor of Gehinnom's fire can easily cause him weakness. When there is no loss of soul, however, the foul odor need not concern us, just as it does not concern us during the weekdays. Therefore, no blessing is recited after Yom Tov, although there is a foul odor, because there is no loss of soul. Similarly, no blessing is recited when Yom Tov begins after Shabbos, although the soul departs, because there is no foul odor. This appears correct. These are his words.
2) There: He recites a blessing over spices, etc. Regarding fragrant wood, one should make the esoteric intention for fragrance explained by us concerning the fragrance of myrtle on Shabbos night itself; see there. Of the two myrtle bundles prepared for Shabbos, as is known, take care when purchasing them that they contain three valid three-leafed myrtle branches. After Shabbos, when reciting Borei Atzei Besamim, take only those three branches in your hand and smell them. These three myrtles should be tied in one knot as a single bundle. Intend that the three myrtles correspond to nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, and intend to retain some of the additional nefesh, ruach, and neshamah added to you on Shabbos. This is accomplished now through these three myrtles and smelling them. It is already known that all actions performed after Shabbos are intended to retain part of the additional Shabbos sanctity for the coming weekdays. Shaar HaKavanos, folio 60b. One should smell the myrtle three times, corresponding to nefesh, ruach, and neshamah. Pri Etz Chaim, gate 18, chapter 24. It appears that even where myrtle is unavailable and the blessing is recited over other spices, one should take three branches of those spices, intending that they correspond to nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, as stated above. See above, siman 216, paragraph 16, for what we wrote regarding the intention for fragrance; see there.
3) One who fasts on Shabbos must recite a blessing over spices, unlike on Yom Kippur. Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos HaTur, paragraph 2; Magen Avraham at the beginning of the siman; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 2. Ginas Veradim, klal 1, siman 8, also agrees; see there. Machazik Berachah, paragraph 1.
4) There: He recites a blessing over spices, etc. When reciting Borei Atzei Besamim after Shabbos, he should hold them in their natural direction of growth. Magen Avraham there in the name of Mahari Weil. If he recites Borei Isvei Besamim or Borei Minei Besamim, which does not mention trees, he need not hold them in their natural direction of growth. Machatzis HaShekel. Nevertheless, the correct practice is to hold even a species that is not woody in its natural direction of growth while reciting the blessing.
5) There: He recites a blessing over spices, etc. Taz writes in Yoreh De'ah, siman 108, paragraph 10, that pepper may be used for Havdalah, contrary to a text he found stating that one should not use pepper for Havdalah after Shabbos; see there. He writes the same in this siman, paragraph 5. This also appears to be Magen Avraham's view at the beginning of the siman. Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos HaTur, paragraph 1, likewise writes that a blessing is recited over crushed pepper; see there. Taz's aforementioned words, however, appear to permit even uncrushed pepper. Olas Tamid, paragraph 1, writes that Knesses HaGedolah's view is correct: specifically crushed pepper may be used because its fragrance is stronger. The same applies to ginger, called imber in the vernacular; a blessing may be recited over it if it is crushed; see there. Nekudos HaKesef there in Yoreh De'ah, however, challenges Taz and writes that Borei Minei Besamim should not be recited over pepper. Furthermore, in cases of doubt regarding blessings we rule leniently; see there. Eliyah Rabbah in this siman, paragraph 1, similarly writes that no blessing should be recited over pepper or ginger, because they are called seasonings rather than spices. He afterward writes that as a matter of practical halachah, perhaps they may be used for Havdalah and a blessing recited over them, but concludes that he lacks authority to be lenient in a case of doubt regarding blessings; see there. Eshel Avraham writes that according to the opinion that pepper is not called a spice, one should recite Hanosein Rei'ach Tov BaPeiros over it, and perhaps there is also no objection if he recites Borei Minei Besamim; see there. See, however, Machazik Berachah, paragraph 5, who discusses the matter and concludes that as a matter of practical halachah, one may recite a blessing over freshly crushed pepper for Havdalah. This is demonstrated and explicitly stated by Responsa Rashba and Maran in the Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah, siman 108, and by Kol Bo, Orach Chaim, Mateh Moshe, and those who follow them. Nevertheless, because of the dispute, one should recite Borei Minei Besamim, as Orach Chaim writes. Mahari Zayin in Responsa Perach Shoshan, klal 1, siman 13, writes the same; see there. Machazik Berachah writes in Kuntres Acharon there that in pressing circumstances, when one cannot crush the pepper, one may rely upon all the aforementioned great authorities and recite a blessing over whole pepper, but should recite Borei Minei Besamim; see there. Shaarei Teshuvah, paragraph 1, cites this. See Sedei Chemed, Asifas Dinim, system of heh, paragraph 13, who appears to agree with Machazik Berachah that in pressing circumstances it may be used for Havdalah; see there.

At a gathering. See Beit Yosef, who notes an apparent contradiction in Tur. The Mechaber rules here as in siman 217, that the prohibition applies specifically at a gathering. In siman 298, seif katan 5, I explained at length that according to Rif and Rosh as well, it applies specifically at a gathering. See there. The reference to siman 239 is a scribal error. If one non Jew and a majority of Jews are reclining there, either the spices belong to the non Jew, in which case this is an ordinary non Jewish gathering, or the spices belong to a Jew, in which case even a majority of non Jews cannot prohibit what is not theirs. See siman 217. With Hashem’s help, this will be explained further in siman 298.
A question. Concerning a valuable, fragrant esrog over which one wishes to recite the blessing on Motzaei Shabbos when no other spices are available, and fruit of orlah became mixed with it in a ratio of less than one to two hundred or more, I discussed this at length in siman 217 in the Magen Avraham section. See Shach, Yoreh Deah, siman 108, seif katan 26, and siman 119, seif katan 27. I also discussed it at length in the laws of festivals. One who is prohibited by a vow from benefiting from another person may not smell his spices, and he may not recite the blessing over that person’s lamp, because this is not a mitzvah for which we say that mitzvos were not given for benefit. See siman 653. It is permitted to smell an esrog designated for the mitzvah, but it is forbidden to smell a hadas designated for the mitzvah, even for Havdalah, because Havdalah is not the mitzvah for which the hadas was designated. A stipulation cannot be made nowadays. See Beit Yosef there. Similarly here, if one recited Havdalah from plag haminchah and then blessed over spices, as in siman 293, one may say that if spices become available on Motzaei Shabbos he should bless again in order to restore his spirit, and this is not a blessing in vain. With Hashem’s help, this will be explained further in Magen Avraham.

Those who don't know, and the Torah and the Rash, in any case, do not give them any permission in that it does not smell: Above, it is simple that there is no division in perfumes to distinguish between herbs that have a good smell or other perfumes, and blesses even herbs if they are dry, as long as they have a good smell:

kaf_hachayyim.he: ה) שם. מברך על הבשמים וכו' כתב הט"ז ביו"ד סי' ק"ח סק"י דפלפל מותר להבדלה ולא כמו שמצאתי כתוב דאין לעשות במו"ש הבדלה על הפלפלין יעו"ש. וכ"כ בסי' זה סק"ה וכ"נ דעת המ"א ריש הסי' וכ"כ השכנה"ג בהגה"ט או' א' דמברכין על פלפל כתוש יעו"ש אכן מדברי הט"ז הנ"ז נראה אפי' אינו כתוש. וכתב העו"ת או' א' דהנכון כדברי כנה"ג דוקא על כתוש שמריח טפי וה"ה זנגביל שקורין בל"א אימביר יכול לברך עליו אם הוא כתוש יעו"ש. אבל הרב נה"כ שם ביו"ד השיג על דברי הט"ז הנ"ז וכתב דאין לברך על הפלפלין בורא מיני בשמים ועוד דספק ברכות להקל יעו"ש. וכ"כ א"ר בזה הסי' או' א' דאין לברך על הפלפלין ולא על הזנגביל משום דנקראו תבלין ולא בשמים אלא שאח"כ כתב לדינא אפשר דמבדילין ומברכין עליהם ומ"מ סיים דאין בידי להקל בספק ברכות יעו"ש. והא"א כתב לברך על הפלפלין הנותן ריח טוב בפירות למ"ד שאין נקרא בשמים ואפשר נמי אם מברך מיני בשמים אין קפידא יעו"ש. אמנם עיין מחב"ר או' ה' מ"ש בזה וסיים דלענין דינא נראה דבפלפל כתוש מקרוב יכול לברך בהבדלה שכן מוכח ומפורש מתשו' הרשב"א ומדברי מרן בש"ע יו"ד סי' ק"ח ולקמן דין ג' ומכלבו ואו"ח ומט"מ וסיעתם אך יברך מיני בשמים הואיל דאיכא פלוגתא כמ"ש האו"ח וכ"כ מהר"י זיין בתשו' בס' פרח שושן כלל א' סי' י"ג יעו"ש עכ"ד. ובק"א שם במחב"ר כתב דבשעת הדחק דאינו יכול לכתוש הפלפילן יש לסמוך על כל הגאונים הנ"ז ולברך על הפלפלין כמו שהן אך יברך מיני בשמים יעו"ש. והביאו שע"ת או' א' ועיין שד"ח באסיפת דינים מע' ה' או' י"ג שכתב דנראה דעתו כהמחב"ר דבשעת הדחק לצורך הבדלה מותר יעו"ש:
kaf_hachayyim.en: 5) There: He recites a blessing over spices, etc. Taz writes in Yoreh De'ah, siman 108, paragraph 10, that pepper may be used for Havdalah, contrary to a text he found stating that one should not use pepper for Havdalah after Shabbos; see there. He writes the same in this siman, paragraph 5. This also appears to be Magen Avraham's view at the beginning of the siman. Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos HaTur, paragraph 1, likewise writes that a blessing is recited over crushed pepper; see there. Taz's aforementioned words, however, appear to permit even uncrushed pepper. Olas Tamid, paragraph 1, writes that Knesses HaGedolah's view is correct: specifically crushed pepper may be used because its fragrance is stronger. The same applies to ginger, called imber in the vernacular; a blessing may be recited over it if it is crushed; see there. Nekudos HaKesef there in Yoreh De'ah, however, challenges Taz and writes that Borei Minei Besamim should not be recited over pepper. Furthermore, in cases of doubt regarding blessings we rule leniently; see there. Eliyah Rabbah in this siman, paragraph 1, similarly writes that no blessing should be recited over pepper or ginger, because they are called seasonings rather than spices. He afterward writes that as a matter of practical halachah, perhaps they may be used for Havdalah and a blessing recited over them, but concludes that he lacks authority to be lenient in a case of doubt regarding blessings; see there. Eshel Avraham writes that according to the opinion that pepper is not called a spice, one should recite Hanosein Rei'ach Tov BaPeiros over it, and perhaps there is also no objection if he recites Borei Minei Besamim; see there. See, however, Machazik Berachah, paragraph 5, who discusses the matter and concludes that as a matter of practical halachah, one may recite a blessing over freshly crushed pepper for Havdalah. This is demonstrated and explicitly stated by Responsa Rashba and Maran in the Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah, siman 108, and by Kol Bo, Orach Chaim, Mateh Moshe, and those who follow them. Nevertheless, because of the dispute, one should recite Borei Minei Besamim, as Orach Chaim writes. Mahari Zayin in Responsa Perach Shoshan, klal 1, siman 13, writes the same; see there. Machazik Berachah writes in Kuntres Acharon there that in pressing circumstances, when one cannot crush the pepper, one may rely upon all the aforementioned great authorities and recite a blessing over whole pepper, but should recite Borei Minei Besamim; see there. Shaarei Teshuvah, paragraph 1, cites this. See Sedei Chemed, Asifas Dinim, system of heh, paragraph 13, who appears to agree with Machazik Berachah that in pressing circumstances it may be used for Havdalah; see there.
